The available evidence does not establish a March 4 snapshot, totals across policy areas, or that AP’s labels changed Trump’s public messaging. The documented proposal was made by the UK government under Prime Minister Keir Starmer. None of the supplied reporting establishes a Trump administration mask ban, U.S. enforcement, or a connection to Donald Trump. The grounded draft therefore describes the UK bill as a proposal at the cited dates and recommends excluding it from a Trump-specific record.

proposal.title: Brennan Center: Project 2025 Proposes Federal Intervention in Local Prosecutors’ Cases
proposal.description_short: The Brennan Center says Project 2025 proposes DOJ intervention in some local prosecutorial choices and efforts to end existing consent decrees.
proposal.description_medium: The Brennan Center’s January 2025 analysis says Project 2025 proposes that the Justice Department charge or intervene against elected local prosecutors over policies it labels “rule of law deficiencies,” including some decisions not to prosecute low-level offenses. The analysis also describes a proposal to eliminate existing DOJ consent decrees. It presents these as plan provisions and risks, not proof that every proposal was implemented.
proposal.description_long: A January 29, 2025 Brennan Center analysis describes criminal-justice proposals in Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation’s policy blueprint for a conservative administration. It says the plan would let the Justice Department charge or intervene against local prosecutors whose policies are labeled “rule of law deficiencies,” including some decisions not to prosecute low-level offenses such as marijuana or shoplifting cases. The analysis also says Project 2025 proposes eliminating existing DOJ consent decrees; it notes that nearly 30 such agreements then covered law-enforcement and jail systems. Consent decrees are court-approved agreements used to remedy unlawful practices, so the Center warns that removing them would reduce federal oversight of local agencies. These are provisions and risk assessments described by the Brennan Center, not proof that all proposals were implemented. The original description’s claims of a permanent constitutional restoration, arrests of opposition leaders, protest bans, revoked citizenship, and forced dissolution of organizations are not supported by the supplied links. The revised account sticks to specific policy proposals and attributes the projected effects to the analysis.

proposal.description_long: In a Senate Judiciary Committee press release, Sen. Dick Durbin, the committee’s ranking member, said he had received whistleblower information about FBI Director Kash Patel’s use and management of bureau aircraft. Durbin characterized the disclosures as alleging that aircraft decisions affected or delayed high-profile investigations, including the Charlie Kirk killing. As an example, he said the FBI shooting-reconstruction team was asked to fly to Utah to assist with the investigation and process the scene. The release does not provide flight logs, a detailed response timeline, or an independent inspector general finding establishing that Patel’s personal travel delayed that team. It does make a separately worded allegation about the FBI’s response to the Brown University shooting, which should not be conflated with the Kirk investigation. The supportable entry is that a senator publicly disclosed whistleblower allegations and described a requested deployment after Kirk’s killing. It should not state as proven fact that personal aircraft use hampered the Kirk response or multiple emergencies. The FBI’s contemporaneous account says agents arrived at the scene within 16 minutes, a distinct fact that further cautions against overstating the alleged delay.

proposal.title: Prosecutors cite Trump social media posts in seeking protective order in Jan. 6 case
proposal.description_short: Prosecutors cited Trump’s social media posts in seeking a discovery protective order in the 2020 election case; the filing was not a finding that the posts were crimes.
proposal.description_medium: In August 2023, special counsel Jack Smith asked the court in Washington to restrict how Donald Trump and his lawyers could disclose materials received in discovery in the 2020 election case. Prosecutors cited Trump’s history of posting about people involved in his cases and pointed to a Truth Social post reading, “If you go after me, I’m coming after you.” Trump’s lawyers argued the post was political speech. The filing documents the prosecutors’ request and stated concern, not a judicial finding that the posts constituted obstruction or witness intimidation.
proposal.description_long: In August 2023, prosecutors in the federal election case against Donald Trump asked a judge in Washington to impose a protective order governing the use and disclosure of discovery materials. The Justice Department argued that public disclosure of evidence such as grand-jury interviews or sealed-warrant materials could chill witnesses or affect the administration of justice. The filing cited Trump’s history of social media posts about judges, lawyers and witnesses in his cases, including a Truth Social message stating, “If you go after me, I’m coming after you.” Trump’s defense described the post as political speech and contested the request. This procedural request concerned access to evidence exchanged in discovery; it was not itself a gag order covering all public statements and did not establish that the posts were criminal conduct. Other reporting in September 2023 described a separate request to restrict statements about participants in the election case. The supplied Washington Post link is an October 2023 catalogue, but its article body was not readable in the focused review. The revised title and account describe the documented protective-order request and avoid an unsupported count of “dozens” or a legal conclusion about obstruction. A final order should be consulted before describing the precise restrictions imposed.

proposal.title: Trump’s Hurricane Maria visit to Puerto Rico included paper-towel distribution
proposal.description_short: Trump’s October 2017 Puerto Rico visit after Hurricane Maria included a paper-towel distribution at a relief center.
proposal.description_medium: Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017. Trump visited on October 3 and tossed paper towels to people at a relief center. GAO later found that staffing, logistics and infrastructure problems complicated FEMA’s response. A George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths through August 2018; this is an excess-mortality estimate, not a count of deaths individually attributed to the storm. The evidence does not connect the paper-towel scene to response delays.
proposal.description_long: Hurricane Maria made landfall in Puerto Rico in September 2017 and caused widespread damage to infrastructure, housing and communications. President Donald Trump visited the island on October 3. During a stop at a relief center, he tossed rolls of paper towels to people gathered there, an action that attracted criticism and became a prominent image of the visit. The federal response faced documented operational problems. The Government Accountability Office later reported that sequential disasters created staffing shortages, logistical challenges impeded the rapid deployment of personnel and supplies, and damage to local systems required FEMA to assume functions normally handled by territorial authorities. Separately, a George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths associated with Hurricane Maria through August 2018; GAO described that figure as Puerto Rico’s then-current official count. “Excess deaths” compares observed deaths with an expected baseline and should not be conflated with a count of deaths individually certified as directly caused by the storm. These sources support the visit, the distribution scene, response challenges and the later mortality estimate. They do not establish that the paper-towel event caused FEMA delays, nor do they provide support for every claim about the Jones Act or funding transfers in the original description. The title is narrowed to the documented visit; the response and mortality context is stated with attribution.

proposal.title: Trump administration suspends enforcement of Biden-era H-2A farmworker rule
proposal.description_short: In June 2025, the Labor Department suspended enforcement of provisions in the 2024 H-2A farmworker rule; the cited action does not concern H-1B visas.

Reuters reported that the rule included protections for foreign agricultural workers, including workplace organizing protections. H-2A covers temporary agricultural work; the cited action does not establish a change to the separate H-1B program for skilled workers. Claims about H-1B restrictions, crop losses or technology-sector labor shortages require separate evidence.
proposal.description_long: On June 20, 2025, the U.S. Department of Labor announced that its Wage and Hour Division had suspended enforcement of provisions introduced by the 2024 H-2A Farmworker Protection Rule. Reuters reported that the Biden-era rule provided protections for foreign agricultural workers in the H-2A temporary visa program, including workplace organizing protections. The Department’s action concerned enforcement of an agricultural labor rule. H-2A visas are for temporary agricultural workers, while H-1B visas cover a distinct category of skilled employment. The linked Reuters story and Labor Department material do not establish that the administration restricted H-1B visas, that employers faced nationwide labor shortages, that crops were wasted, or that technology companies suffered losses. The prior title grouped H-2A and H-1B programs together and therefore implied a broader change than the cited action supports. This revised account is limited to the reported suspension of enforcement of the H-2A rule and identifies the program distinction. The material does not explain every legal consequence of the suspension or establish that all protections were permanently removed. Any description of later litigation, reinstatement or H-1B policy changes should rely on separate dated sources.

proposal.description_long: On July 29, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized revisions to federal regulations governing coal-combustion residuals, or coal ash, from electric utilities.
